newsitem.title: USA: Psoriasis treatment can lead to skin cancer - study.
newsitem.headline: Psoriasis treatment can lead to skin cancer - study.

text.p: The most effective treatment for the skin disease psoriasis can also cause deadly skin cancer, according to a study in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine.

But doctors are likely to continue using the treatment, a combination of ultra violet light and a drug, because there is no better way available to help psoriasis sufferers, an editorial in the Journal said.

Experts recommended doctors monitor their psoriasis patients closely for signs of cancer, which can take up to 15 years to appear and turned up even in patients who had not received psoriasis treatments for several years.

The finding poses a quandary for people suffering from psoriasis, a common and sometimes inherited skin condition that includes itchy, scaly red patches, usually on the elbows, forearms, legs and scalp.

A medical research group led by Dr. Robert Stern of Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center found that people who had received at least 250 treatments with the combination of ultraviolet A light and the medicine psoralen were five times more likely to develop malignant melanoma.
The skin tumors seem to arise about 15 years after the first treatments begin.

The combination of invisible ultraviolet A light and psoralen, also known as methoxsalen and sold under the brand name Oxsoralen by ICN Pharmaceuticals, is an extremely effective treatment for psoriasis. The treatment is also known as PUVA (Psoralen and UltraViolet A).

The Stern team followed 1,380 people who received the treatment at 16 university medical centers in 1975 and 1976. By 1991 they had noticed a cluster of skin cancer cases among people who had received more than 280 treatments.

Analysis showed the number of malignant melanoma tumors was far more than expected after 1991 and that the skin cancer was striking 5.4 times more people than expected. The more treatments a patient received, the higher the risk.

"The increased risk of malignant melanoma that begins 15 years after the first PUVA treatment and is associated with a high level of exposure is a reason for caution in the long-term use of this therapy, especially in young people and those in early middle age," the researchers concluded.
Patients who have received the treatment, they said, should be checked regularly for skin cancer.

In an editorial, Dr. Klaus Wolff of the University of Vienna in Austria called the results "alarming, because melanoma is fatal if left untreated." Two of the nine melanoma patients in the Stern study died from the cancer.

"Even more alarming is the fact that in this study melanomas appeared only after a long latency period, which suggests that more patients treated with PUVA in the past may have melanomas in the future," Wolff said.
He added that "none of the patients in whom melanoma developed had received PUVA for at least five years, which suggests that the risk persists after treatment is stopped."
Yet because the treatment "offers innumerable patients the chance to resume a normal life," said Wolff, a comparison of the risks and benefits suggests "we cannot for now afford to abandon PUVA."

People who have received PUVA treatments should be examined regularly, he said, and patients who would have had a higher-than average risk for melanoma without the treatments "should not be given this treatment," he said.
